query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A non-equilibrium, rapidly solidified Mg-containing lightweight HEA (with density <6 g/cm³) initially forms as a supersaturated single-phase material but then evolves via diffusion-driven phase separation upon exposure to high-temperature or corrosive environments. In this evolution, segregation and nucleation of stable intermetallic compounds (for example, Ti-rich or mixed Mg intermetallic phases) occur, which locally alter the electrochemical landscape and promote the development of a more protective, passivating oxide film. This microstructural evolution is responsible for the enhanced corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: A rapidly solidified, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA (e.g., a Mg–Ti–Zn system) processed to a density below 6 g/cm³, exhibiting a homogeneous, supersaturated single-phase microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subjecting samples to controlled post-processing exposure (either via thermal aging at oxidation temperatures, e.g., ~800°C, or via prolonged exposure to a chloride-containing corrosive solution at room temperature) to induce phase separation.
generation.conditions: Comparative tests between as-cast (baseline) and post-exposure (aged) samples. Oxidation tests at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800°C) and corrosion tests in standard NaCl solutions at room temperature (or other relevant corrosive media) under controlled exposure times.
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation and growth of stable intermetallic compounds (such as Ti-rich or Mg-stabilized phases) that segregate at grain boundaries or defect sites.
generation.mechanism: Rapid solidification traps a metastable supersaturated solution; subsequent environmental exposure (thermal or corrosive) drives diffusion and localized segregation. This results in the precipitation of stable intermetallic phases that in turn alter local chemical potentials and oxide formation kinetics. The intermetallic phases act as preferential sites for forming a protective, passivating oxide layer by either reducing microgalvanic coupling or by contributing beneficial elements (e.g., Ti) to the oxide scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, aged samples will display a measurable increase in secondary intermetallic phase fraction, particularly at grain boundaries, accompanied by a shift toward a more noble corrosion potential and lower corrosion current densities, as well as thicker or more adherent oxide scales in high-temperature oxidation tests.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing HEA with a uniform, metastable single-phase microstructure that exhibits poorer corrosion resistance and less stable high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to lightweight HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ and is valid for processing conditions that yield a metastable supersaturated structure. The effect is expected provided that the alloy has sufficient diffusivity to allow phase separation and that the environmental exposure (thermal or corrosive) falls within typical test conditions (e.g., ~800°C for oxidation; standard NaCl solution at room temperature for corrosion).
generation.uncertainty: The specific identity and volume fraction of the intermetallic compounds, as well as the exact magnitude of the improvements in corrosion/oxidation performance, may vary with precise alloy composition and processing conditions. Further detailed optimization is required to generalize the findings across different Mg-based HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing HEA samples produced via rapid solidification (with density <6 g/cm³). Subject one set to controlled thermal aging (e.g., holding at 800°C for a predetermined time) or prolonged corrosive exposure (e.g., immersion in a NaCl solution) to induce phase evolution, while keeping the other set as-cast. Characterize both sets via microstructural (XRD, SEM/EDS) analysis, corrosion testing (potentiodynamic polarization), and high-temperature oxidation tests.
measurements: Phase composition and fraction of intermetallic compounds (using XRD and SEM/EDS)
Surface oxide scale morphology and thickness after oxidation tests
Corrosion potential and corrosion current density measurements from electrochemical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show an increased fraction of stable intermetallic phases and fail to display an improved corrosion behavior (i.e., no shift to more noble corrosion potential and no reduction in corrosion current density) or enhanced high-temperature oxide scale stability relative to the as-cast baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), which include multiple principal elements, have attracted substantial research attention due to their exceptional mechanical properties, such as high fracture toughness, hardness, fatigue and corrosion resistances, yield strength, ductility and thermal stability,,,. In many applications, HEAs can significantly outperform traditional and super-alloys, especially at low and high temperatures,. Recently, the design of lightweight HEAs (with a density lower than 5 g/cc) has become one of the hottest research topics in metallurgy. In view of the outstanding performance of HEAs, the lightweight HEAs may have superior performance than traditional lightweight materials such as Al, Mg, and Ti alloys, with a large number of potential industry applications. Yet the chemical and compositional design space of HEAs is exceptionally vast, which makes the use of the traditional experimental methods for HEA screening an overwhelming task. Thus, an efficient, accurate strategy is required for the design of lightweight HEAs for specific applications,. The aim of the present work is to investigate the influence of systematic variations in Mg content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of these alloys. By characterizing the resulting intermetallic phases, grain refinement, and passive film formation, this study identified how processing and composition synergistically affect the corrosion resistance and mechanical performance. This work offers new insights into the design of corrosion-resistant, high-strength materials and represents a novel extension of compositionally complex alloy design to Mg-rich systems.
